Title: A matrix and its transpose have the same set of eigenvalues/other version: $A$ and $A^T$ have the same spectrum
Content: Let $ \sigma(A)$ be the set of all eigenvalues of $A$ . Show that $ \sigma(A) = \sigma\left(A^T\right)$ where $A^T$ is the transpose matrix of $A$ .
AcceptedAnswer: The matrix $(A - \lambda I)^{T}$ is the same as the matrix $\left(A^{T} - \lambda I\right)$ , since the identity matrix is symmetric. Thus: $$\det\left(A^{T} - \lambda I\right) = \det\left((A - \lambda I)^{T}\right)  = \det (A - \lambda I)$$ From this it is obvious that the eigenvalues are the same for both $A$ and $A^{T}$ .

To prove that $\sigma(A) = \sigma(A^T)$, we recall that the spectrum $\sigma(A)$ is the set of all eigenvalues $\lambda$ satisfying $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$. 

Consider the characteristic polynomial of $A^T$:  
$$\det(A^T - \lambda I).$$  
By Assumption 2, we have:  
$$\det(A^T - \lambda I) = \det((A - \lambda I)^T) = \det(A - \lambda I),$$  
where the last equality holds because the determinant of a matrix equals the determinant of its transpose.  

Thus, $\det(A^T - \lambda I) = \det(A - \lambda I)$ for all $\lambda$. Consequently, $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ if and only if:  
$$\det(A - \lambda I) = 0 \iff \det(A^T - \lambda I) = 0,$$  
meaning $\lambda$ is also an eigenvalue of $A^T$. Therefore, the sets of eigenvalues are identical: $\sigma(A) = \sigma(A^T)$.
